## Linear Covariance Propagation

Let's look into how linear covariance propagation works and the benefits of using it. In state estimation, two important quantities are the 
mean, $\mathbf{x}$, and the covariance, $\mathbf{P}$. The covariance represents the uncertainty in the state estimate. Imagine a bell curve, representing a 1-dimensional distribution; the 
covariance reduces to variance and represents how "wide" the bell curve is, where a larger covariance correlates to a "wider" bell curve.

With this in mind, let's look at a scenario involving two satellites in formation flight. Let's call the satellite being followed the "Chief" and the following satellite the "Deputy". In this 
scenario we will assume the state of the Chief satellite is perfectly known, while the Deputy has some covariance associated with its state estimate as seen in @fig-formation. 

![Chief-Deputy formation flight geometry. *Diagram generated with Gemini.*](images/formation_flight.jpg){#fig-formation width="80%" fig-align="center"}

As the two satellites progress in their orbits, the covariance can also be propagated forward to show the uncertainty in the Deputy's state over time using linear covariance propagation. 
@eq-lincov is the equation used for performing this propagation.

$$
\mathbf{P}(t) = \mathbf{\Phi}(t,t_0) \mathbf{P}_0 \mathbf{\Phi}(t,t_0)^T + \mathbf{Q} 
$${#eq-lincov}

In this equation, $\mathbf{\Phi}$ represents the state transition matrix, which uses linearized dynamics to propagate state deviations from $t_0$ to $t$. 
$\mathbf{P}_0$ is the covariance at $t_0$, and $\mathbf{Q}$ represents process noise to account for unmodeled perturbations, though in our scenario this will be zero because we will be modeling the system using two-body equations of motion with the only perturbation being gravity.
 @eq-lincov will do a good job at propagating the covariance forward in time given that the uncertainty remains Gaussian and that the linearized dynamics contained 
 in $\mathbf{\Phi}$ accurately represent the true system dynamics. Linear covariance propagation saves time by eliminating the need for large Monte Carlo simulations to analyze the uncertainty bounds.
